c01.display: Welcome back to NLP, Simply Explained. This is unit 2, lesson 3: chunking.
c01.spoken: Welcome back to N L P, Simply Explained. This is unit 2, lesson 3: chunking.

c02.display: Last time we tagged every word as a noun, a verb, and so on. Today we group those words into small phrases.
c02.spoken: Last time we tagged every word as a noun, a verb, and so on. Today we group those words into small phrases.

c03.display: Here's the idea. Chunking groups words into small, useful phrases, without working out the full grammar of the sentence.
c03.spoken: Here's the idea. Chunking groups words into small, useful phrases, without working out the full grammar of the sentence.

c04.display: A chunk is a short group of words that acts as one unit, such as a noun phrase. Chunks sit side by side and never overlap.
c04.spoken: A chunk is a short group of words that acts as one unit, such as a noun phrase. Chunks sit side by side and never overlap.

c05.display: In "the big red bus stopped near my old school", the chunks are: the big red bus, stopped, near, and my old school.
c05.spoken: In "the big red bus stopped near my old school", the chunks are: the big red bus, stopped, near, and my old school.

c06.display: Think of reading aloud. You naturally group words into bite-sized pieces, one breath at a time, without stopping to diagram the sentence.
c06.spoken: Think of reading aloud. You naturally group words into bite-sized pieces, one breath at a time, without stopping to diagram the sentence.

c07.display: Each chunk gets a type. Let's label our sentence.
c07.spoken: Each chunk gets a type. Let's label our sentence.

c08.display: The big red bus is a noun phrase, NP for short: a noun with the words that describe it.
c08.spoken: The big red bus is a noun phrase, N P for short: a noun with the words that describe it.

c09.display: Stopped is a verb phrase, VP.
c09.spoken: Stopped is a verb phrase, V P.

c10.display: Near is a preposition, which links the bus to where it stopped.
c10.spoken: Near is a preposition, which links the bus to where it stopped.

c11.display: And my old school is another noun phrase.
c11.spoken: And my old school is another noun phrase.

c12.display: Here's a clever trick. We can turn chunking into a tagging job, just like part-of-speech tagging, using three letters.
c12.spoken: Here's a clever trick. We can turn chunking into a tagging job, just like part-of-speech tagging, using three letters.

c13.display: B means this word begins a chunk.
c13.spoken: B means this word begins a chunk.

c14.display: I means this word is inside the chunk that's already started.
c14.spoken: I means this word is inside the chunk that's already started.

c15.display: And O means the word is outside any chunk, like a full stop.
c15.spoken: And O means the word is outside any chunk, like a full stop.

c16.display: Let's tag a short sentence: "The big bus stopped", with a full stop.
c16.spoken: Let's tag a short sentence: "The big bus stopped", with a full stop.

c17.display: The begins a noun phrase, so it's B-NP.
c17.spoken: The begins a noun phrase, so it's B dash N P.

c18.display: Big is inside that noun phrase: I-NP.
c18.spoken: Big is inside that noun phrase: I dash N P.

c19.display: Bus is still inside it: I-NP.
c19.spoken: Bus is still inside it: I dash N P.

c20.display: Stopped begins a verb phrase: B-VP.
c20.spoken: Stopped begins a verb phrase: B dash V P.

c21.display: And the full stop is outside every chunk, so it gets O.
c21.spoken: And the full stop is outside every chunk, so it gets O.

c22.display: There are two ways to build a chunker.
c22.spoken: There are two ways to build a chunker.

c23.display: A rule-based chunker uses patterns over part-of-speech tags. For example: a determiner, then any adjectives, then a noun, makes a noun phrase. It's easy to read, but real text often breaks the rules.
c23.spoken: A rule-based chunker uses patterns over part-of-speech tags. For example: a determiner, then any adjectives, then a noun, makes a noun phrase. It's easy to read, but real text often breaks the rules.

c24.display: A learned chunker is a tagger that predicts B, I and O for each word, using many clues at once. It needs labelled examples to learn from, and today it's the usual choice.
c24.spoken: A learned chunker is a tagger that predicts B, I and O for each word, using many clues at once. It needs labelled examples to learn from, and today it's the usual choice.

c25.display: So what are chunks good for?
c25.spoken: So what are chunks good for?

c26.display: They find the things a text talks about: people, places and products are usually noun phrases.
c26.spoken: They find the things a text talks about: people, places and products are usually noun phrases.

c27.display: They help pull out simple facts. Apple, bought, a startup: who did what to what.
c27.spoken: They help pull out simple facts. Apple, bought, a startup: who did what to what.

c28.display: And they're a quick first step towards full parsing, which builds the complete structure of a sentence. That's coming up in unit three.
c28.spoken: And they're a quick first step towards full parsing, which builds the complete structure of a sentence. That's coming up in unit three.

c29.display: Quick quiz. In BIO tagging, which tag does the word red get, in "the big red bus"?
c29.spoken: Quick quiz. In BIO tagging, which tag does the word red get, in "the big red bus"?

c31.display: It's I-NP. The word "the" begins the noun phrase, and big, red and bus are all inside it.
c31.spoken: It's I dash N P. The word "the" begins the noun phrase, and big, red and bus are all inside it.

c32.display: Let's recap. A chunk is a short group of words that acts as one unit.
c32.spoken: Let's recap. A chunk is a short group of words that acts as one unit.

c33.display: The most common are noun phrases and verb phrases.
c33.spoken: The most common are noun phrases and verb phrases.

c34.display: B, I and O tags turn chunking into a tagging job.
c34.spoken: B, I and O tags turn chunking into a tagging job.

c35.display: And chunks help find the things a text talks about, and simple facts about them.
c35.spoken: And chunks help find the things a text talks about, and simple facts about them.

c36.spoken: Next lesson: Generative vs Discriminative. Should a model learn how data is made, or just where the boundary is?
